input: During a late shift he became shaky and struggled to read a docket, then ate a snack without assistance and felt better, but no glucose was checked until nearly an hour later, when the meter displayed 6.2 mmol/L.

There is no documented persistent reading, no verified four-week period of control and no recent specialist report; the nurse records possible glucose-related symptoms and variable pressure measurements without assigning a definite cause or choosing one reading as representative.
Blood-pressure treatment was increased two weeks earlier after several elevated home readings, and he reports brief light-headedness when standing without a definite blackout.

Today's BP 162/96 mmHg is a single seated observation; the nurse has not attributed the visual complaints to blood pressure, established persistent hypertension from the available entries or treated the unreliable field result as a confirmed measurement.

The driver reports that vehicles approaching from the left sometimes appear suddenly, although he can read the central letters on a chart and denies constant double vision; he also describes occasional overlapping headlights after long night shifts, which were absent during the consultation.
He recalls being told that an old injury left one eye less useful, while an earlier letter records vision in both eyes and no current specialist opinion confirms monocularity.
A handwritten acuity entry of 6/9 is not assigned to an eye or labelled as corrected, and the driver alternates between an older pair of glasses and a recently purchased pair during work.
He also mentions occasional blurred vision when his glucose changes, but an eye card with corrected 6/6 in each eye is more than a year old and no current retinal or visual field report is available.
